candidate.answerReason: Root-coefficient identities and squared-difference inequalities force a ≥ 3√3. Equality is attained by (x − √3)^3, and at that value the inequalities force b = 9, agreeing with B.

methods.label: Bound the coefficients using the roots
methods.explanation:
The same coefficient \(a\) appears twice, suggesting a relation between the sum and product of the roots. First, the roots must be positive: for \(x\le0\), every term of \(x^3-ax^2+bx-a\) is nonpositive and the constant term is strictly negative, since \(a,b>0\). Thus no nonpositive number is a root.

Write the three real roots, including multiplicity, as \(r,s,t>0\). Expanding their linear factors gives
\[
(x-r)(x-s)(x-t)
=x^3-(r+s+t)x^2+(rs+rt+st)x-rst.
\]
Here choosing one constant term from the factors produces the coefficient of \(x^2\), choosing two produces the coefficient of \(x\), and choosing all three produces the constant term. Comparing coefficients yields
\[
r+s+t=rst=a,
\qquad rs+rt+st=b.
\]
To eliminate the individual roots, use the identity
\[
(u+v+w)^2-3(uv+uw+vw)
=\frac{(u-v)^2+(v-w)^2+(w-u)^2}{2}
\ge0.
\]
Applying it first to \(r,s,t\) gives \(a^2\ge3b\). Applying it to \(rs,rt,st\), whose pairwise products sum to \(rst(r+s+t)=a^2\), gives
\[
b^2\ge3a^2.
\]
Because \(a,b>0\), this means \(b\ge\sqrt3a\). Combining the bounds and dividing by \(a>0\),
\[
a^2\ge3b\ge3\sqrt3a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a\ge3\sqrt3.
\]
This lower bound is attainable, since
\[
(x-\sqrt3)^3
=x^3-3\sqrt3x^2+9x-3\sqrt3
\]
has three real roots counted with multiplicity and has positive coefficients \(a=3\sqrt3\), \(b=9\).

Finally, when \(a=3\sqrt3\), our bounds require
\[
9=\sqrt3a\le b\le\frac{a^2}{3}=9.
\]
Thus \(b\) is uniquely \(9\). Equality in the first squared-difference identity also forces \(r=s=t=\sqrt3\), because a sum of nonnegative squares can vanish only when every square vanishes. The answer is \(\boxed{9}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).

review.mathematicalCheck: The polynomial is strictly negative for nonpositive inputs, so all real roots are positive. Coefficient comparison gives sum and product \(a\), and pairwise-product sum \(b\). The squared-difference identities yield \(a^2\ge3b\) and \(b^2\ge3a^2\), forcing \(a\ge3\sqrt3\). The displayed cube attains this bound, where the bounds uniquely force \(b=9\).
